data.title: The Cividale Gospel Book – Pribina, Koceľ, Rastislav and Svatopluk
data.excerpt: The Cividale Gospel Book is among the most important sources for the beginnings of Slavic history, and its margins carry the names of Svatopluk, Rastislav, Koceľ and Pribina. From the beginning of the second half of the 9th century the monks of Aquileia entered in it the names of the distinguished visitors to their monastery.

children.text: THE CIVIDALE GOSPEL BOOK is among the most important sources relating to the beginnings of Slavic history, and especially to that of the Slovaks, Bulgarians, Croats and Slovenes. It contains the names of our rulers in the Early Middle Ages - Svatopluk, Pribina and Rastislav. Like many other such monuments, it too has until now not been available online in good quality.

The original text of the Cividale Gospel Book was probably written between the 4th and the 7th century in the Aquileian village of Monastero. For a long time one part of the gospel book — the Gospel of St Mark — was regarded as his authentic manuscript. Today we know that it is only one of many copies. Its exceptional historical importance, however, lies in the marginal entries of the names of distinguished visitors to the monastery mentioned. The making of the entries of names of Great Moravian and Pannonian provenance can essentially be dated to the beginning of the second half of the 9th century. It is assumed that the monks of Aquileia, out of gratitude for the gifts brought to them and out of respect for the visitors, hit upon the idea of entering their names in the most sacred of books. The entering of names continued roughly from the 8th to the 10th century. And so, alongside Lombard and Byzantine rulers, as well as other dignitaries and perhaps also merchants from various parts of Europe, there appear entries of Slavic names such as: Svatopluk, Svätožizňa, Predslav, Rastislav, Koceľ, Pribina, Michael, Sondoke, Braslav, Trpimír. The entries suggest that the distinguished visitors used the monastery of Aquileia as a convenient place to rest after long journeys, which led chiefly to Rome and Venice. In the gospel book the names are at first entered in the order of the folios. Later, however, once the space in the margins of the first folios had been used up, the spaces between the lines of the biblical text itself also began to be used unsystematically.
